tagline.text: A southern Ivatan village on Sabtang with limestone houses and cogon roofs

location.label: Location
location.text: Brgy. Chavayan, southwest coast of Sabtang Island, Batanes

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500~3,500 (Sabtang day round trip, including boat, tricycle and small spending; flights excluded)

children.text: Chavayan is a small Ivatan village tucked between the mountains and the sea on the southwest side of Sabtang Island, where traditional stone houses with thick limestone walls and cogon-grass roofs survive in their most complete form. You can also watch vakul being woven at the weavers' association and visit a seaside chapel.

Chavayan is one of the six barangays of Sabtang, a municipality in Batanes, and a very small village set between the mountains and the sea on the island's southwest side. Sabtang is among the southernmost inhabited islands of Batanes, the northernmost province of the Philippines, and Chavayan lies at the island's southern end, facing the northern tip of Luzon. The 2024 census counted 158 residents, slightly fewer than the 169 recorded in 2010. At that size you can walk the whole village in about an hour.

The village name is said to come from cha, meaning bountiful, and vay, the word for the arrowroot plant. The biggest draw is the stone houses the Ivatan call sinadumparan. They have thick walls built of powdered limestone and coral and a roof of cogon grass, a style said to have been introduced under Spanish rule in the late 1800s, and some houses are more than 100 years old. The provincial government has declared this village and Diura in Mahatao cultural zones to protect their architecture.

What makes Chavayan special is that it has practically no commercial buildings and no nearby cell site, so daily life stays close to tradition. Farming and fishing are the main livelihoods, and a separate traditional Ivatan kitchen still stands beside the houses. This is less a tourist attraction than a living village to walk through quietly, so respect for residents' homes and daily routines matters when you take photos.

Sabtang island tours usually treat Chavayan as just one quick stop. But if you walk it slowly in the early hours before the sun climbs, taking in the weavers' hut, the seaside chapel and the stone-house lanes in turn, the day on Sabtang feels much deeper. Unlike the Sabtang Island entry that covers the whole island, this guide focuses on Chavayan alone: a walking order, costs and cautions.

Houses with thick walls of limestone and coral dust and cogon-grass roofs line the narrow lanes. Some are over 100 years old and people still live in them, so look from the lane and do not step inside. On an overcast morning the limestone looks softest in the light.

blocks.title: Welcome rotunda and Sabtang Weavers Association

children.text: Beside the welcome rotunda at the village entrance stands the small hut of the Sabtang Weavers Association. You can watch older women weave vakul and soot, and the hut also sells handicrafts such as abaca bags, purses, baskets (pasikin) and salakot hats.
The vakul is a palm-fibre headdress and cape that Ivatan women wear over the head and back. One blog says renting one for photos costs about

per person (2019 and 2024 posts agree; confirm locally), while vakul to buy cost much more, from a few hundred to over a thousand pesos depending on size. The kanayi, a man's shoulder soot, reportedly takes three weeks to a month to make.
This small chapel with a pastel facade and cogon roof stands about

from the beach. Villagers built it between 1951 and 1959 through yaru, communal work similar to bayanihan, and it is described as the only church on the islands still in its traditional form. Residents also pray here before dawn before going out to fish or farm.

Ireneo Hornedo, who led the building of the chapel, is also said to have built the village theater (teatro) and the welcome rotunda. The theater is used for local events and shows how the community built things by its own effort.

blocks.title: Kissing Rocks and Monument of Satisfaction

children.text: Two rock formations on the beach that seem to lean together are called the Kissing Rocks, and a natural rock formation on the cliff is called the Monument of Satisfaction. Both are close to the village and make good photo stops on a walk.
A small store at the far end of the village (avuyi) reportedly sells chavayanas, the native sandals fishermen wear. Some visitors buy a pair as a souvenir because it carries the village's name.

items.subtitle: Spend a night in the village

children.text: Arrive on Sabtang early, leave your bag at your lodging and find a tricycle. It helps to ask your host in the evening to arrange the next day's tricycle.
Pass the Chamantad-Tinyan Viewpoint and the coast road and enter Chavayan. Around sunset the beach and the area around the chapel are quiet.
Walk the chapel and the stone-house lanes in the quiet hours. Watch from a distance and do not disturb residents at dawn prayers or heading out to farm.
See vakul and soot being made at the weavers' association and buy a souvenir. Then head up toward Savidug or go back to the port in time for your boat.

The dry season from March to May is the best time for Chavayan. The sea is calm, so boats are rarely cancelled, and the weather is steady for walking the stone houses and the beach. December to February is cool, but northeast winds can make the sea rough on some days.
June to November is the rainy and typhoon season. High waves can stop boats for days, and if your return boat is cancelled your plans fall apart. If you go then, leave spare days.

Chavayan is described as having a few homestays in traditional stone houses, but there are very few rooms and rates and opening status differ from source to source, so ask locally in advance. If you plan to sleep on Sabtang, book early, get a contact number before you arrive and carry plenty of cash. Sleeping in a stone house is considered a highlight of a Sabtang trip, but many places have simple or shared showers and toilets.

The village has almost no commercial buildings, so do not expect restaurants or convenience stores. Eat lunch at a restaurant in another Sabtang village or ask your lodging to prepare it in advance. Ask your host beforehand whether meals are possible and what is served, and some visitors report asking residents for a coconut to eat while walking the village. Prepare water and snacks near the port.
Taking the first boat to Sabtang and arriving early gives you the quietest village and the softest light.
Boat and tricycle fares differ from source to source, so confirm the current fares locally and bring plenty of cash.
Do not just watch at the weavers' association; buying a handicraft helps the village.
When photographing in front of stone houses, greet the residents first and ask permission before photographing people or the inside of a home.
The village reportedly has no cell site, so download your maps and arrange how to stay in contact beforehand.
Prices for vakul rental and souvenirs vary by seller, so ask the price before you take photos.
Check your return boat time and the weather, and move your schedule earlier if the waves are high.
Pack a hat, sunscreen, water and a light rain jacket. Long sleeves are good on windy days.

Boats to Sabtang are cancelled depending on wave height and are cut especially often from June to November. If your return boat is blocked you may have to stay a day or more on the island, so leave slack in your plans.
Chavayan is a village where people live, not a tourist facility. Do not enter homes or photograph residents without permission.
There are almost no lodgings, restaurants or shops, so prepare food and cash beforehand.

Some sources say boat fares, entry procedures and environmental charges change over time, so check the latest notices at the Sabtang tourist information center or the Batanes tourism office before you leave.
Reports say old stone houses are being replaced by concrete ones, so respect the efforts to preserve the old houses and do not touch or climb on heritage structures.
Sources describe Chavayan's UNESCO World Heritage status in conflicting ways, so it is best not to state it as confirmed.
The island Chavayan belongs to, with Savidug, the Chamantad-Tinyan Viewpoint, a lighthouse and more that you can visit together. From the port you reach Chavayan by tricycle.
Another village with well-preserved old stone houses, on a hillside with narrow lanes. It is best walked early in the day.
